# The independent median-pair target need not have a convex Ball body

This is a counterexample to a proposed auxiliary property, not to (OC).
It applies to the explicit independent left/right median-pair target and
fails at its **unique** deepest point.

## The mixed-integer body and its median target

Work with one integer coordinate and two continuous coordinates. Put

\[
 A=\{(x,y):|x|+|y|\le1\},\qquad B=\varepsilon A,
 \qquad K=[-1,1]^2,\qquad \varepsilon=\frac14,
\]

and let

\[
 C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((\{-1\}\times A)
       \cup(\{0\}\times K)\cup(\{1\}\times B)\bigr).
\]

This is a full-dimensional compact convex body in \(\mathbb R^3\).
Its only integer fibers are exactly \(A,K,B\), at indices \(-1,0,1\).
Indeed, the endpoint fibers are exact because their indices are extreme,
and
\[
 (A+B)/2=((1+\varepsilon)/2)A\subset K.
\]
Any convex combination at index zero consists of a point in \(K\)
and an equal-weight combination of the endpoint fibers, so the middle
fiber is also exact.

Their areas are
\[
 a=2,\qquad k=4,\qquad b=2\varepsilon^2=\frac18,
 \qquad M=a+k+b=\frac{49}{8}.
\]
The unique weighted median integer index is zero: both strict-side masses
are less than \(M/2\), whereas at either endpoint the opposite strict-side
mass is greater than \(M/2\).

Let \(X,Y\) be independent uniform points in \(A,B\), respectively.
The segment between \((-1,X)\) and \((1,Y)\) meets the middle fiber at
\(Z=(X+Y)/2\). The proposed median-pair target is
\[
 d\eta(x,y)=1_K(x,y)\,dx\,dy+b\,d\operatorname{Law}(Z)(x,y).
\]
It has total mass \(k+b=33/8\).

## Exact density of the paired component

Use coordinates \(p=x+y\), \(q=x-y\), whose absolute Jacobian determinant
is two. Under the uniform law on \(A\), \(p,q\) are independent uniforms
on \([-1,1]\); under the uniform law on \(B\), they are independent
uniforms on \([-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\).

Define
\[
 \ell=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2},\qquad R=\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2},
\]
and the one-dimensional convolution density
\[
 h(t)=\begin{cases}
 1,&|t|\le\ell,\\
 (R-|t|)/\varepsilon,&\ell\le|t|\le R,\\
 0,&|t|\ge R.
 \end{cases}
\]
This is the density of \((U+V)/2\) for independent uniforms
\(U\in[-1,1]\), \(V\in[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\): the convolution
overlap length gives the displayed plateau and two linear shoulders.
Its integral is \((1-\varepsilon)+\varepsilon=1\).

Consequently the target has the density
\[
 f(x,y)=1_K(x,y)+4\varepsilon^2 h(x+y)h(x-y). \tag{1}
\]
The factor two converting the \((p,q)\)-density to the \((x,y)\)-density
is included here.

## The origin is its unique deepest point

The density (1) is invariant under \((x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)\). It is
absolutely continuous and at least one throughout the square. Every line
through zero has zero target measure, and inversion exchanges its two
closed halfplanes. Thus each such halfplane has measure \(\eta(\mathbb R^2)/2\).
Every halfplane containing zero contains a through-zero halfplane, so
zero has depth exactly half the target mass.

If \(w\ne0\), put \(u=w/|w|\). The halfplane
\(\{x:u\cdot x\ge|w|\}\) contains \(w\), but has measure strictly less
than the half mass in \(\{x:u\cdot x\ge0\}\). The intervening open slab
has positive measure, because the density is positive on a neighborhood
of zero. Hence \(w\) has smaller depth. This proves uniqueness, including
points outside the support.

## Exact Ball radial body and failure of convexity

For definiteness use the normalization
\[
 \mathcal B_f=\{r u:u\in\mathbb S^1,\ 0\le r\le\rho(u)\},
 \qquad \rho(u)^2=2\int_0^\infty t f(tu)\,dt. \tag{2}
\]
Changing the conventional constant in (2) only dilates the body, so it
does not affect convexity.

For \(\varepsilon<s<1\), use the nonunit direction \(v_s=(1,s)\).
Along this ray the square contributes for \(0\le t\le1\). On the support
of \(h(t(1+s))\), we have
\[
 t(1-s)\le R\frac{1-s}{1+s}\le\ell,
\]
where the last inequality is exactly \(s\ge\varepsilon\). Thus the
second convolution factor equals one on that support. It follows that
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 I(s)&:=\int_0^\infty t f(t,st)\,dt\\
 &=\frac12+\frac{4\varepsilon^2}{(1+s)^2}
                      \int_0^R t h(t)\,dt.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The remaining elementary integral is
\[
 J:=\int_0^R t h(t)\,dt
   =\frac{\ell^2}{2}+\frac{\ell\varepsilon}{2}
                        +\frac{\varepsilon^2}{6}
   =\frac18+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{24}.
\]

The radial boundary on this sector is therefore
\[
 P(s)=r(s)(1,s),\qquad
 r(s)=\sqrt{2I(s)}=\sqrt{1+\frac{c}{(1+s)^2}},
 \quad c=8\varepsilon^2J=\varepsilon^2+\frac{\varepsilon^4}{3}
                          =\frac{49}{768}. \tag{3}
\]
For clarity, (3) also follows directly from (2) by homogeneity of the ray
integral, so no unit-direction Jacobian is missing.

Write \(t=1+s\). Differentiating (3) gives
\[
 r'=-\frac{c}{t^2\sqrt{t^2+c}},\qquad
 r''=\frac{2c}{t^3\sqrt{t^2+c}}
                  +\frac{c}{t(t^2+c)^{3/2}},
\]
and hence
\[
 r r''-2(r')^2=\frac{3c}{t^2(t^2+c)}>0. \tag{4}
\]
If \(X(s)=r(s)\), \(Y(s)=s r(s)\), then
\[
 Y'(s)=r+s r'=\frac{t^3+c}{t^2\sqrt{t^2+c}}>0.
\]
The boundary in this sector is consequently a smooth graph \(X=\phi(Y)\),
and the chain rule gives
\[
 \phi''(Y(s))
 =\frac{r r''-2(r')^2}{(r+s r')^3}>0. \tag{5}
\]

Here this is the local **right-hand** boundary. One may check this
directly: in the open sector \(\varepsilon<Y/X<1\), membership in
\(\mathcal B_f\) is equivalent to
\[
 Q(X,Y):=X^2-1-\frac{cX^2}{(X+Y)^2}\le0.
\]
On the boundary, writing \(s=Y/X\), we have
\[
 Q_X=2X\left(1-\frac{c s}{X^2(1+s)^3}\right)>0,
\]
because \(X^2=1+c/(1+s)^2\) and
\(c s<(1+s)((1+s)^2+c)\). Thus points immediately to its right are
outside the radial body.

Fix any \(s_0\in(\varepsilon,1)\). For sufficiently small \(h>0\), take
the two boundary points with ordinates \(Y(s_0)-h\) and \(Y(s_0)+h\).
By (5), their midpoint has ordinate \(Y(s_0)\) and abscissa strictly
greater than \(\phi(Y(s_0))\). Taking \(h\) sufficiently small keeps this
midpoint in the neighborhood where \(Q_X>0\), so it is outside
\(\mathcal B_f\). Both endpoints are in the body. The radial body is
therefore nonconvex.

Since the origin is the target's unique deepest point, choosing a
different deepest point cannot repair the failure. This disproves the
proposed universal convexity of the two-dimensional Ball body of the
independent median-pair target about one of its deepest points.
